card.hook: Picture a cream-white hotel with green shutters, sitting calmly while scooters buzz past on the pavement. That's the Sofitel Legend Metropole, and it's one of the easiest buildings in Hanoi to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand on the public pavement of Ngô Quyền Street, right in front of the main entrance and the white portico with the hotel's name on it. Face the building and shift a step or two until the whole façade sits nicely in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if the pavement is narrow, because it fits the whole front and portico in. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the engraved name and the green shutters.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the portico up with the centre line, then tap the white wall and nudge it a touch darker so the white doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to a white façade than harsh midday sun. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a wall.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the pavement right outside the main entrance at 15 Ngo Quyen Street, with the hotel frontage behind you. A travel page calls this area a popular photo hotspot. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and let the white façade fill the background over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street side across from the hotel's front entrance, so the whole white façade and green shutters fit behind you while you pose by the entrance.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the public pavement. The courtyard, pool and interior are for hotel guests, so please don't go into the grounds for pictures. Pavements get busy with cars, scooters and people, so look around before you step back for a wider shot.
card.challenge: Get a perfectly straight, symmetrical shot of the façade with a sliver of pavement at the bottom, then find the tiniest detail you can, like the name on the portico, and zoom in on it.
card.good_to_know: The hotel opened in August 1901 as the Grand Métropole Hôtel, then the largest and most modern hotel in French Indochina. Somerset Maugham stayed in 1923, Charlie Chaplin and Paulette Goddard honeymooned here in 1936, and Graham Greene stayed in 1951. Today's hotel was rebuilt and reopened in 1992. If you have time, walk round to Lý Thái Tổ Street for a second frame of the newer Opera Wing next to the Hanoi Opera House.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the public pavement of Ngô Quyền Street, right in front of the main entrance and the white portico with the hotel's name on it. Face the building and shift a step or two until the whole façade sits nicely in the frame.

card.hook: Three arches, one dead-straight line, and a temple that's been around since 1070. Your first photo here is the easy one, so start with it.
card.stand_here: Stand outside at Văn Miếu Môn, in front of the main entrance gate and right on the central axis. Face north, with the gate square in front of you and the temple grounds beyond it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the gate straight on. If the whole facade won't fit, tap 0.5x. Once you're inside, try 2x or more (it depends on your phone) for close-ups of the stelae and the turtle bases.
card.make_it_pop: Switch the gridlines on, line up the middle arch, then tap the brightest part of the gate and slide a little darker so the facade doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the sun lights the gate facade from the east. Paths inside can fill up, so early also helps you wait for gaps between visitors.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit back so the landmark fits over your shoulder. Keep the gridlines on so you both stay level.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate can be photographed from outside, but the compound is ticketed, so check the official site before you go for entry and opening details. Turn flash off in the worship halls.
card.challenge: Find the round windows on the red upper storey of the Khuê Văn pavilion and get them all in one frame, ideally with the Thiên Quang well reflecting them back.
card.good_to_know: The Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu) was first built in 1070. From 1076 to 1779 it also housed the Imperial Academy, Vietnam's first national university. Eighty-two stone stelae on turtle bases survive, naming 1,307 graduates from royal exams held between 1442 and 1779.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand outside at Văn Miếu Môn, in front of the main entrance gate and right on the central axis. Face north, with the gate square in front of you and the temple grounds beyond it.

card.hook: Picture a calm grey granite building with a sloping roof, two guards at the door and lawns laid out in neat green squares. It's about as tidy as a Hanoi photo gets, and you barely have to try.
card.stand_here: Head for the open lawns on the north-facing front approach in Quảng trường Ba Đình (Ba Đình Square). The mausoleum is to the west, straight ahead of you, so face it head-on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front. Drop to 0.5x if you want the lawn and flagpole big in the foreground, and keep your phone level so the sides don't lean. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is good for the carved name over the entrance and the guards at the door.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the base of the building on the lower line, then tap the facade and slide it a touch darker so the pale sky doesn't wash out the grey granite.
card.best_time: Early morning is best, with low sun and thinner crowds. The flag-raising is at 6 a.m. in the hot season and 6:30 a.m. in the cold season. Late afternoon is also soft and quieter, and if you stay for the 9 p.m. flag-lowering, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the green lawns of Ba Đình Square, in front of the mausoleum, so the building sits behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the whole facade fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the square facing the building, so the whole facade and plaza fit in the frame, while you stand on the lawn in front of the mausoleum with it behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine outside on the square and in the gardens, but not inside. Ask before photographing the guards, and don't climb or lean on anything for a shot. Selfie sticks are generally not allowed inside the complex, so check with staff on the square. Barriers can close parts of the square, so use whatever view is open.
card.challenge: Get the building perfectly centred and level, with a path between the lawn squares leading straight to the door. Then see if you can do it with a guard in the frame and nobody wandering through.
card.good_to_know: The mausoleum is about 21.6 metres high and 41.2 metres wide. Work began in 1973 and it was inaugurated in August 1975. The design drew on Lenin's Mausoleum in Moscow, but adds a Vietnamese sloping roof.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the open lawns on the north-facing front approach in Quảng trường Ba Đình (Ba Đình Square). The mausoleum is to the west, straight ahead of you, so face it head-on.

card.hook: Picture a vermilion-red bridge floating over calm green water, with trees leaning in around it. That's the one shot everybody comes to Hoàn Kiếm Lake for, and it's easy to get on a phone.
card.stand_here: Stand on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, on the lake's north/east side, and face the red Huc Bridge. From the drop-off in the historical centre, the lake lies to the west, about 2 minutes on foot. Use the map to find the exact spot along the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the bridge sits small and clear in the middle distance. Try 0.5x for more trees and sky, or 2x to bring the bridge and Jade Islet closer without walking.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then drag the slider to make it slightly darker so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunrise, or after dark when the bridge is lit (switch on night mode and rest your phone against a railing or your body to keep it steady). Both times are popular, so expect crowds, especially at weekends.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a little higher and further out. That way the landmark fits over your shoulder behind your smile.
card.rules_and_safety: The lake shore is open public space, and you don't need a temple ticket for the shore views. If you want to go onto Jade Islet or into Ngọc Sơn Temple, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take a second picture from Lê Thái Tổ and see if you can catch the little Turtle Tower peeking through the shoreline trees.
card.good_to_know: Hoàn Kiếm means "Lake of the Returned Sword". Legend says Emperor Lê Lợi gave a magic sword back to a Golden Turtle God here after winning a war against Ming China. The Huc Bridge's name is poetically translated as "Perch of the Morning Sunlight", and it leads to Jade Islet and the 18th-century Ngọc Sơn Temple.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, on the lake's north/east side, and face the red Huc Bridge. From the drop-off in the historical centre, the lake lies to the west, about 2 minutes on foot. Use the map to find the exact spot along the street.

card.hook: Scooters buzz past a thick old brick wall, and behind it is the only bit of a once-huge prison that's still standing. It's a plain, weathered subject, and the busy street around it makes it feel properly Hanoi.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner where Hai Bà Trưng Street meets Hỏa Lò Street, on the gate side of the prison. The prison lies to the south-west of you, so face that way and you'll see the wall and gate at an angle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the wall, the gate and the street into one shot, then go to 1x for a more natural look. Try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gate and the Maison Centrale sign without stepping into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, run the wall along one line and let the gate sit off-centre, so the street leads the eye towards it.
card.best_time: Daylight is simplest, and earlier in the day is usually calmer. Check the museum's official site for visiting times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the pavement in front of the gatehouse with the 'Maison Centrale' facade behind you, and use the front camera at 0.5x so the whole gate fits over your shoulder. For a splash of colour, try beside the long stone wall on Hỏa Lò Street, where one traveller saw red flags and lanterns hanging from the trees.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Hỏa Lò Street facing the front gate while you stand on the pavement in front of the gatehouse, so the full gate fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Stay on the pavement and keep an eye on the traffic while you line up your shot. Inside the museum, photos are generally fine in daytime, but flash is restricted and some areas are off-limits, so follow the staff's guidance. Don't block walkways.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole street scene and one tight shot of the Maison Centrale sign, then see which one your friends like more.
card.good_to_know: The French built Hỏa Lò Prison between 1896 and 1901 and called it Maison Centrale, or 'Central House'. Later, American prisoners of war nicknamed it the 'Hanoi Hilton'. Hỏa Lò means 'stove', after the street where stove-sellers once traded. The prison was demolished in 1993-94, and only the gatehouse remains, as a museum.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner where Hai Bà Trưng Street meets Hỏa Lò Street, on the gate side of the prison. The prison lies to the south-west of you, so face that way and you'll see the wall and gate at an angle.

card.hook: Picture a small grey tower sitting all alone on green water, with Old Quarter roofs behind it and absolutely no way to walk up to it. That's Turtle Tower, so every photo is taken from the shore.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Đinh Tiên Hoàng and Lê Thái Tổ, at the southern end of the lake where the two streets meet. Face out across the water and you'll see the tower on its islet, with the Old Quarter roofline behind it.
card.zoom: Start at 2x and go up to 5x if your phone has it, which brings the tower nicely closer. Use 1x when you want a wider scene with more lake and rooftops. Skip 0.5x here, because it shrinks the tower to a speck.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the tower on one third of the screen and leave open water in front so the reflection shows. Then tap the tower and slide the brightness down a little so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset gives you warm light on the tower and its reflection. Early or late in the day the water is usually calmer too, so the reflection looks cleaner and the colours are softer.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, so more of the scene fits in. Turn your back to the view and keep the landmark over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your face and take a few, because the first one is rarely the best.
card.rules_and_safety: The islet can't be visited, so shoot from the lakeside. Check the weekend walking-street schedule before you go, as it can change how busy the shoreline is.
card.challenge: Take one shot with a patch of empty lake in the foreground and the reflection showing, then one at 5x. Which tower looks calmer?
card.good_to_know: The tower was built in 1886 in honour of Lê Lợi, the national hero linked to the lake's sword-and-turtle legend. In 1890 the French put a miniature Statue of Liberty on top. It was taken down in 1945.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Đinh Tiên Hoàng and Lê Thái Tổ, at the southern end of the lake where the two streets meet. Face out across the water and you'll see the tower on its islet, with the Old Quarter roofline behind it.

card.hook: Eleven red tiers poke up above the trees, and the lake wraps right around the little islet they sit on. It's one of the calmest-looking pictures in Hanoi, even with the traffic behind you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Đường Thanh Niên, at the approach to the stone causeway. Face the temple entrance and the red stupa, with the lake filling the bottom of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic view of the stupa with water in front. Go to 0.5x for more water and sky, but keep the stupa away from the edges, where it can look stretched. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for just the red tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the stupa on one of the vertical lines, and leave a strip of lake along the bottom.
card.best_time: Late afternoon gives warm light on the red tower, but sunset is busy, so be ready to wait for a clear view. Early morning is quieter and can bring mist over the lake.
card.selfie_here: Walk into the grounds and stand under the Bodhi tree with the red stupa behind you. Visitors call it a hot spot for photos. Or use the lakeside walkway, face out over West Lake with the stupa behind you, and use the front camera (try 0.5x to fit more in).
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand on the stone walkway from Thanh Niên Road toward the entrance and aim at the red stupa with the lake in front, while you stand between them so the stupa is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an active place of worship, so cover your shoulders and knees. Photos are fine outside, but not inside the prayer halls or during ceremonies. Skip the flash and don't photograph worshippers up close. Check opening hours locally, as night access to the grounds may be restricted.
card.challenge: Get the stupa straight and upright on a gridline with no scooters in the frame. Take a few shots in a row, because the causeway is busy.
card.good_to_know: Trấn Quốc is the oldest Buddhist temple in Hanoi. It was first built in the sixth century under Emperor Lý Nam Đế, then moved to this islet in 1615 when the Red River began eating into its old site. The Bodhi tree in the grounds grew from a cutting of the tree at Bodh Gaya in India, given in 1959.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Đường Thanh Niên, at the approach to the stone causeway. Face the temple entrance and the red stupa, with the lake filling the bottom of your screen.

card.hook: Columns, a decorated roofline and a balcony dead centre: the Hanoi Opera House pretty much poses for you. It's one of the easiest buildings in the city to photograph, and the open square out front gives you room to get it all in.
card.stand_here: Stand in Quảng trường Cách mạng Tháng Tám (August Revolution Square), on the open forecourt directly in front of the main façade. Face the building and step back until the columns and roofline fit in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close to the building, then switch to 1x once you've backed away across the square. Try 2x or higher for details like the columns, balcony and roofline (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Evening or sunset is best, when the façade is floodlit. Go early in the morning if you'd like fewer people in the square.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps to the main entrance and stand slightly to one side, so the columns and arched windows fit behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the building rises over your shoulder. Or stand on the open paved forecourt with the building behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the corner near the Hilton Hanoi Opera hotel on Lê Thánh Tông Street, across the square, while you pose in front of the building so they can get the full façade.
card.rules_and_safety: The Opera House has been closed for renovation since 31 January 2026. The outside and the square can still be photographed, but scaffolding or fencing may affect your view, so check before you go. Skip the flash. Don't step into the traffic lanes: it's a busy intersection with lots of motorbikes, so cross slowly and steadily.
card.challenge: Can you get the whole roofline in the frame with the balcony right in the middle and a little strip of square at the bottom?
card.good_to_know: The Opera House was built between 1901 and 1911, modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris but smaller, with materials chosen to suit Hanoi's climate. It seated 870 people. Its balcony is where Viet Minh leaders proclaimed independence in September 1945.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Quảng trường Cách mạng Tháng Tám (August Revolution Square), on the open forecourt directly in front of the main façade. Face the building and step back until the columns and roofline fit in the frame.

card.hook: Picture a tiny wooden shrine balanced on one stone pillar, floating over a lotus pond like a flower on a stem. That's exactly what it's meant to look like, and it's much easier to photograph than most famous sights.
card.stand_here: Stand at the pond edge directly in front of the shrine, centred on the pillar, and face the pagoda. Step back along the edge a little so the whole pillar and roof fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the pillar and roof sit nicely in the frame. If you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x and keep the pagoda near the middle so the edges don't stretch it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the pillar on the centre vertical line, then tap the pavilion and drag the slider down a touch to make it darker so the sky doesn't wash out the roof.
card.best_time: Go early, about 7-9 am, when the light is good and the pond is calmer. The pond edge gets crowded by mid-morning.
card.selfie_here: Try the quiet courtyard behind the pagoda, in the corner by the bodhi tree and the small altar. It's often empty, and you can use the front camera at 0.5x to squeeze the trees and pagoda in behind you. Check the framing on the spot, as the pagoda may not sit right over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the front edge of the pond, facing the shrine, while you stand on the pond rim in the foreground with the pagoda centred above its reflection.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine outside the shrine, but keep flash off inside, and shoes come off before you go in. Don't block the stairs or narrow paths, and ask before photographing worshippers. The pond edge is narrow and can be slippery after rain, so mind your footing.
card.challenge: Wait for the ripples to settle, then catch the pagoda and its twin in the water in one calm, perfectly centred shot.
card.good_to_know: Emperor Lý Thái Tông first built the pagoda in 1049, and it was perfected in 1105. It was destroyed in 1954 and rebuilt in 1955, so what you see is a careful restoration. The shape is a lotus, a Buddhist symbol of purity because it flowers in muddy water.

card.hook: Picture a red arched bridge crossing still water to a tiny temple island, with a stone Pen Tower close by to frame it. It's one of those scenes that looks good even on a hazy day.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lakeside path on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, near the Pen Tower (Tháp Bút). Face south across the water: the Thê Húc Bridge and the temple island are straight ahead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the bridge, the water and the Pen Tower together. Try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge and temple roofs. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the Pen Tower to look tall and close.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then slide the brightness a little darker so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Around 6 PM is suggested for golden-hour light, and early morning works for the bridge at sunrise. These times come from visitor tips, so check the light on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to Đắc Nguyệt Lâu (the Moon Gazing Pavilion) at the island end of Thê Húc Bridge. Stand under the gate with the bridge behind you, use the front camera, and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the scene in.
card.ask_someone: Near the Lý Thái Tổ statue on the western lakeshore path, the bridge sits nicely against the green island behind it, so it's worth asking a passer-by to take your photo there (have a look at the view first).
card.rules_and_safety: Entering the temple grounds is ticketed, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone away inside the main hall and near the altar, and don't point it at people who are praying.
card.challenge: Put the Pen Tower on one side of the frame and the red bridge on the other, with the horizon dead level. Gridlines will help you get it right.
card.good_to_know: Ngọc Sơn Temple was built in the early 19th century and was first dedicated to the "Three Sages". The national hero Trần Hưng Đạo was brought into the temple later. The Pen Tower, the ink-slab, the Đắc Nguyệt pavilion and the Trấn Ba pavilion all carry symbolic meaning.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lakeside path on Đinh Tiên Hoàng, near the Pen Tower (Tháp Bút). Face south across the water: the Thê Húc Bridge and the temple island are straight ahead.

card.hook: The front of Đồng Xuân Market is a bit of a show-off: five proud arches, with motorbikes, vendors and shoppers streaming past like extras in your photo. Grab your spot, take a breath and wait for the gap.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map is at the market itself, but the middle of the building is inside, so walk out to the street in front of the main entrance. Stand there and face the five arches.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole five-arch front in. If traffic or crowds stop you stepping back, tap 0.5x. Use zoom 2x or higher for close-ups of the arches, signs or goods.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the centre arch up with the middle of the frame and keep your phone upright so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daytime shows the facade most clearly, and early in the day the street may be calmer. On Friday to Sunday evenings the street in front has been closed to traffic for the night market, so it can be easier to frame and well lit, but check locally that this still applies. After dark, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady.

card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing people or stalls, as vendors may not want to be in your shot. Watch for passing motorbikes when you step back, and wear closed-toe shoes because it's wet and dirty outside the main building.
card.challenge: Take five quick shots and pick the one where the street is busy but nothing blocks your centre arch.
card.good_to_know: Đồng Xuân is the largest covered market in Hanoi. The French administration built the first market here in 1889. A fire in 1994 nearly destroyed it, and it was partly rebuilt in its original form.

card.hook: Most city gates have a bus stop or a billboard stuck to them, but Đoan Môn just has open sky. That makes it one of the easiest big photos you'll take in Hanoi.
card.stand_here: Stand in front of Đoan Môn, the main gate, on the south side facing the entrance, and give yourself room to step back. The citadel grounds stretch out behind the gate to the north-west.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x to fit the whole gate in when you're close, or step back and use 1x for a more natural look. Save zoom 2x-5x for the carved dragons at Điện Kính Thiên (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the gate up square so the roofline stays level, then keep a band of sky above it.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, when the grounds are quiet and the light falls on the gate from the east. Sunrise or sunset can also give you strong shadows.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the southern facade of Đoan Môn, the spot guides and reviewers name as the top photo backdrop. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the gate rise up over your shoulder. For a second option, shoot from ground level at the foot of the stone dragon steps at Kinh Thiên Palace.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed, but flash is discouraged in the covered archaeological section and drones generally need a permit. Parts of the site have uneven stone and low steps, so watch your footing when you pose on the steps. It's a ticketed site with its own opening days, and some areas may be closed for archaeological work or events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the stone dragons on the steps at Điện Kính Thiên and fill your whole screen with just one dragon's carved scales. Bonus points if a friend can guess which part of the dragon it is.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1010 under Emperor Lý Thái Tổ and finished in early 1011. It stayed the seat of the Vietnamese court until 1789. Much of it was later pulled down under the French, so today you see surviving gates, restored buildings and open archaeological ground. The central sector became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.

card.best_time: Check how the light hits the façade on the day, since that decides when it looks best. Skip Sunday evening around the 6:00 PM Mass if you want a clear view, because crowds fill the square and the street.
card.selfie_here: Head into the front square and stand in the middle of the semi-circle, beside the bronze Virgin Mary statue inside the railings. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tilt up so both towers sit over your shoulder. Check the angle on the spot.

card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the outside and the square are fine any time. Inside, stay quiet, don't photograph people who are praying, and skip flash during services. The square gets crowded, so keep an eye on your phone and belongings.
card.challenge: Take five frames while the scooters roll by, then find the one where both towers are clear and the street looks tidy for exactly one second.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1884 and the cathedral was consecrated in December 1886, which makes it the oldest church in Hanoi. The towers are about 31 m high and each holds five bells. It stands on the site of the old Báo Thiên Pagoda, and the outside was restored between July 2020 and May 2022.

card.hook: Picture a rusty steel giant with a patched-up look, and then the whole thing starts to shake as a train rolls across it. That's Long Biên Bridge, and the shaking is part of the fun.
card.stand_here: Stand on Đường Trần Nhật Duật, on the stretch facing the bridge's Hanoi-side approach. Face the bridge so the steel framework fills your view and you've got space for a train to cross.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the girders and the train in one frame. Try zoom 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pull a passing train closer to the steelwork. When you walk onto the bridge, switch to zoom 0.5x to stretch the steel lattice into the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the steel along one third of the frame, then tap the train or the brightest part of the sky and slide a little darker so the steel looks bold and the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go around sunrise or sunset. The low golden light throws strong shadows across the steelwork. Trains cross several times a day, so take a few shots as one approaches rather than waiting for one perfect moment.
card.selfie_here: Try the platform by Long Bien railway station, reached from the parking lot at the foot of the bridge. Guides rank it as the most popular spot on the bridge, and the steel structure ends up behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and keep the steelwork over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sandbank of the middle island, Bãi Giữa, while you stand a little way off so the full bridge fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the pedestrian lanes and never step onto the rails for a photo. Sources differ on how safe the platform is and trains can leave little time to step clear, so only use it when no train is near. Bãi Giữa is for the dry season only, never after heavy rain, and not alone after dark. Check the official site for any restoration work or restrictions before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a train crossing with the steel on one third of your frame, then see if you can spot the old girders and the newer repairs in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: The bridge was built between 1899 and 1902 and opened in 1903 as Paul Doumer Bridge. At about 2.4 km, it was then one of the longest bridges in Asia. It was bombed heavily during the Vietnam War, and only about half of it keeps its original shape.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Đường Trần Nhật Duật, on the stretch facing the bridge's Hanoi-side approach. Face the bridge so the steel framework fills your view and you've got space for a train to cross.

card.hook: Most city squares are crowded with stuff. Ba Đình Square is the opposite: huge lawns, one very tall flagpole and a pale granite building, with sky doing the rest. It's a calm, tidy picture, and that's the charm.
card.stand_here: Stand in Quảng trường Ba Đình at the southern end, right by the flagpole, and face north. The mausoleum is about 117 m to the west, so check the framing on site and turn until the facade rises over the lawns with the flagpole in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the flagpole and the mausoleum facade in one shot. Go to 0.5x for the full spread of the lawns, then zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the guards or the flag-raising.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the flagpole on one vertical line, then tap the facade and slide the brightness a touch darker so the pale granite keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 9 a.m., when the facade is lit from the front instead of backlit. Some guides also say the square is quieter then. If you can, catch the morning flag-raising, when the guards in white uniforms stand out against all that open space.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the tall flagpole at the southern end of the square. It's 25 meters high and a popular photo spot. Use the front camera, switch to its wider setting if your phone has one, and check on screen what's behind you before you tap.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine on the square but not inside the mausoleum. Ask before photographing a guard on duty, stay off the grass, and leave the drone at home, because drones are banned in the government district. The mausoleum has security screening, a dress code, bag restrictions and closing days, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the flagpole sitting neatly on a gridline with the whole mausoleum behind it, and not a single stray lawn-walker in the shot?
card.good_to_know: Ho Chi Minh read the Proclamation of Independence here on 2 September 1945. The square is named after the Ba Đình Uprising against the French in 1886-1887. It's about 488 m across, and the granite mausoleum was built on it after his death.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Quảng trường Ba Đình at the southern end, right by the flagpole, and face north. The mausoleum is about 117 m to the west, so check the framing on site and turn until the facade rises over the lawns with the flagpole in front.

card.hook: Quán Thánh Temple gives you three easy photos within a few steps of each other: the gate and roofline, the lake behind the entrance, and a shady courtyard under a giant banyan tree. Start at the gate, then wander.
card.stand_here: Stand on Thanh Niên Road, slightly south of the temple, on the lakeside road. Face the entrance, with the temple just to the east, so the gate and roof fill the front and West Lake sits behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and roofline with the lake behind. If the whole gate won't fit from the roadside, tap 0.5x. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is great for roof ridges and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the gate and roof on the lower third, and keep the phone level so the roof lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Early morning is best from this angle. If the bright lake makes the temple look dull, tap the gate and slide the brightness until the carving looks right.
card.selfie_here: Try the temple forecourt, standing in front of the Tam Quan (triple entrance) gate with the arched gate behind you. A travel guide calls it a popular photo spot, but treat it as a fallback. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit higher so the gate fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from Thanh Niên Road, a little south of the main gate, while you stand by the gate, so the roofline and lake show behind you. Check it on site.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of worship, so keep out of worshippers' way and don't photograph people while they pray. Turn off your flash near altars and take your shoes off before the raised prayer areas. Photos inside the main shrine may cost a fee, so check before you go. Next door is a military base, so skip photos of that building.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the gate sits on the lower third, the roof lines are dead straight and the lake peeks out behind it. Bonus points if nobody's elbow sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: Quán Thánh is a Taoist temple beside West Lake, dedicated to Trấn Vũ, a guardian deity of the north. Tradition dates it to the 11th century, and it's one of the Four Sacred Temples said to protect the old capital. Inside is a black bronze statue of Trấn Vũ, cast in 1677 and almost four metres tall, while the gate and shrine were last rebuilt in 1893.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Thanh Niên Road, slightly south of the temple, on the lakeside road. Face the entrance, with the temple just to the east, so the gate and roof fill the front and West Lake sits behind them.

card.hook: Quick, name the country: a bright yellow palace with classical columns, a grand staircase and wrought-iron gates. Surprise, it's Hanoi, and the only obvious local touch is the mango trees.
card.stand_here: Stand on Hùng Vương street, outside the palace gates on the frontage at 2 Hùng Vương, and face west toward the building. Check any signs first, because photographing the front from outside may be restricted.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if you're close to the gates and want the whole yellow front and the ironwork in one shot. Switch to 1x for a natural look, or 2x or more (depends on your phone) to pick out the columns and broken pediments without stepping closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the gates along the bottom third, tap the yellow wall, then drag the brightness down a touch so the yellow stays rich instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, when the light falls nicely on the facade. Yellow wall, black ironwork and green trees do the colour work for you.
card.selfie_here: Use the roadside opposite the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum, not the footpath in front of the building, and take the selfie with the yellow facade behind you. If the grounds are open, the small bridge over the carp pond is a great alternative with the yellow walls and trees behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stand back from the gate on the street side, near the main entrance area, and ask someone to shoot from the street so the whole yellow palace fits in.
card.rules_and_safety: Don't point your phone at security posts or restricted areas, as photography near them isn't allowed. Signs on the day come first, and the grounds may need a ticket and aren't open every day, so check the official site.
card.challenge: Find the one thing that says 'Vietnam' in this very European scene (hint: it has mangoes) and get it in your frame with the yellow wall.
card.good_to_know: The palace was built between 1900 and 1906 as the home of the French governor-general of Indochina. After 1954 Ho Chi Minh is said to have chosen not to live in it, and built a stilt house and a carp pond in the gardens instead. Today it's used for state occasions, and the building is closed to visitors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Hùng Vương street, outside the palace gates on the frontage at 2 Hùng Vương, and face west toward the building. Check any signs first, because photographing the front from outside may be restricted.

card.hook: Two golden dragon heads guard a pale yellow building with a red pagoda-style roof, and they're begging to be in your photo. Give them the front row.
card.stand_here: Walk to the front of the main entrance at 1 Tràng Tiền, right by the two golden dragon heads. Face the building so the yellow walls and tiered red roof rise up behind the dragons.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade, the roof and both dragon heads in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for roof tiles and balcony details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the yellow wall, then drag the slider to make the picture a touch darker so the sky and the golden dragons keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go in daylight hours, when the front is well lit. Sun and shadow on the walls and balconies add depth.
card.selfie_here: Stand between the two golden dragon heads with the main entrance behind you. A travel guide picks these ornaments out as a stylish backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the yellow facade and red roof fit over your shoulder. For a calmer backdrop, the outdoor courtyard has stone sculptures with the yellow facade behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the street side in front of the entrance, so the full yellow facade and its row of old trees fit in the frame, while you pose near the golden dragon heads.
card.rules_and_safety: Entry to the galleries is ticketed, and photo rules inside may differ from outside, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch one dragon head in the bottom corner of your frame with the red roof rising behind it, like the dragon is showing off the building.
card.good_to_know: This began as the Musée Louis-Finot, which opened in 1910 and was redesigned between 1925 and 1932 by architects Ernest Hébrard and Charles Batteur. Its mix of French colonial and traditional Vietnamese design is called "style Indochinois". It became a public museum in 1958 and now holds around 200,000 items, from the Stone Age to the 1945 revolution.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the front of the main entrance at 1 Tràng Tiền, right by the two golden dragon heads. Face the building so the yellow walls and tiered red roof rise up behind the dragons.

card.hook: Three square brick tiers, a pointy little pyramid on top and a red flag flying above it all. The Flag Tower of Hanoi has such a clear shape that it's hard to take a bad photo of it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Điện Biên Phủ street and step back from the tower toward the street, so the whole thing fits against the sky. The tower is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east, so face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the tower and the flag both fit. Go to 0.5x if you're closer in, to catch the stepped base. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for the flag against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, tap the tower, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky stays blue and the flag stays red.
card.best_time: Morning is lovely, with soft light on the brick. Late afternoon is a good second choice.
card.selfie_here: Walk the stepped terraces at the base, then back up toward the street side of the tower on Điện Biên Phủ (number 28A) so the tower and flag sit behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the red flag over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Lenin Park, directly across the street, so they can fit the whole tower in view across the road, while you pose on the tower side.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb on the walls or railings. The tower sits in the old Vietnam Military History Museum grounds, and access to the inside and upper levels can change, so plan on photographing the outside.
card.challenge: Can you keep the tower perfectly straight, with the flag at the top and a strip of sky above it? Phone level, no leaning tower!
card.good_to_know: The tower is 33.4 m high, or 41 m with the flag. It's thought to date from 1805 or 1812, when it served as an observation post for the Hanoi Citadel. It came through the French attack of 1896-1897 without being destroyed.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Điện Biên Phủ street and step back from the tower toward the street, so the whole thing fits against the sky. The tower is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east, so face north-east.
